1191.title: Sariputra transformed
1191.hook: the goddess switches bodies with Sariputra to show that male and female are not fixed
1191.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read the goddess's exchange with Shariputra as a lesson on emptiness, that no form is fixed, and some modern Buddhist writers also draw on it in discussions of women in Buddhism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heavenly flowers slid off the bodhisattvas and clung to the disciples who called them improper. Your line: the flowers stick.

Shariputra is still sitting there with petals on his robe, and he has a question for the goddess. She's clearly wise; she's just out-talked him about the flowers. So he asks: why don't you change out of your female form? Some readers hear behind it an old view that certain attainments weren't open to a woman as a woman. To him, the question sounds reasonable. The goddess answers it twice: once with words, and once with his own body.
screen: `PETALS STILL ON HIS ROBE.` → `WHY NOT CHANGE YOUR FORM?` → `SHE ANSWERS TWICE.`

segments.voice: First the words, paraphrased. I've looked for the marks of being female, she says, and I haven't found them. So what would I change? Suppose a magician conjures up a woman. Would you ask the illusion to change her form? No, says Shariputra; an illusion has no fixed form to change. Just so, says the goddess. Nothing has a fixed form. Then the second answer. By her power, she turns Shariputra into a likeness of herself, and herself into a likeness of Shariputra. Now the goddess, in his form, asks Shariputra, in hers: why don't you change out of your female form? Bewildered, he answers: I don't know how I turned into this. If you could change out of it, she says, then everyone in a woman's form could change. You aren't a woman, yet you appear as one. In the same way, all who appear as women aren't women in some fixed, final way. The Buddha taught that all things are neither male nor female. Then she lets him go back. Where is your female form now, she asks. It isn't anywhere, and it isn't nowhere, says Shariputra. That's how it is with all things, she says. Afterward Vimalakirti tells him this goddess has served many Buddhas and can take whatever birth she wishes. A few weeks ago, the Lotus had the dragon king's daughter changing form to make a point. Here the question is turned around on the one asking it. The label he was sure of turns out not to be fixed.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a label you wear, or one you've put on someone: the shy one, the difficult one, too old for that. Ask what the goddess asked: where exactly is it? Look for where it begins and ends, and notice whether it's as solid as it sounded.
Sariputra transformed. The goddess swaps forms with him to show that male and female aren't fixed, and asks why he doesn't change back. Today's word.
Your line: not fixed. Even the one asking the question can change shape. Same time tomorrow.

1192.title: The thunderous silence
1192.hook: asked about non-duality, the bodhisattvas answer in words; Vimalakirti stays silent
1192.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists read Vimalakirti's silence as a teaching about the limits of words, and in Chan and Zen communities it is retold as a model of answering without explaining.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a goddess swapped forms with Shariputra, and the label he was sure of came loose. Your line: not fixed.

A question goes around a room, and everyone gets a turn. One by one, the guests in Vimalakirti's sickroom give their answers, each one careful and good. Then the question comes back to the host, the sick layman lying on his couch. The room waits. And he says nothing at all. No shrug, no smile, no meaningful look. Just nothing. And the guest who asked him, the bodhisattva of wisdom himself, calls that nothing the real answer.
screen: `A QUESTION GOES AROUND THE ROOM.` → `EVERY GUEST ANSWERS.` → `THE HOST SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question. Vimalakirti asks the bodhisattvas gathered around him: how does a bodhisattva enter the teaching of non-duality? The doorway, the sutra calls it. They answer one at a time. Each names a pair the mind is used to splitting, birth and death, self and other, pure and impure, this world and nirvana, and shows how the pair isn't really two. It's a lovely, patient stretch of the sutra, answer after answer, each one true. Then they turn to Manjushri. Non-duality, he says, is where nothing is spoken, explained, pointed to or known. It's beyond every word. Then he turns to the host: we've all given our answers; now you tell us. And Vimalakirti is silent. Excellent, excellent, says Manjushri. This is the real entry into non-duality, where words and letters have no place. Here's the difference. Manjushri's answer was right, but he still had to use words to say it. Vimalakirti's silence doesn't describe the doorway. It walks through it. Some later readers in East Asia call it a silence like thunder. And it isn't the silence of someone who doesn't know, or someone sulking, or dodging. It comes last, after every other answer has been said in full, in reply to a real question. The silence lands because of all the words before it. In daily life, it can be the moment after a friend finishes telling something hard, when any answer would make it smaller.
screen: `PAIRS DISSOLVED, ONE BY ONE.` · `MANJUSHRI: BEYOND ALL WORDS.` · `VIMALAKIRTI SAYS NOTHING.` · `A SILENCE LIKE THUNDER.` · then, large: `THE THUNDEROUS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself one plain question: what is here, right now? Let the answers rush in, words and labels and little explanations, and set each one down without arguing. Then ask again and don't answer at all; just stay with the sounds, the weight of the body, the breath going in and out.
The thunderous silence. Vimalakirti's wordless answer to the question of non-duality, given after every other answer had been spoken. Today's word.
Your line: thunderous silence. Sometimes the fullest answer has no words in it. Until tomorrow.

1193.title: Indra's net
1193.hook: a net of jewels in which each jewel reflects every other (Flower Garland, as Huayan explains it)
1193.howItsDone: In the Huayan tradition of China, and in schools that grew from it in Korea and Japan, Indra's net is a classic teaching image for how all things contain and reflect one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti answered by saying nothing at all, and later readers heard thunder. Your line: thunderous silence.

Dew hangs on a spider's web at sunrise. Lean in close to one drop and there's the whole garden inside it, tiny and curved. Lean closer and the next drop over is in there too, and inside that drop is this one. Two drops, each holding the other. Now let that run across the whole web. Remember Fazang's golden lion, and the lamp in a room of mirrors? Today, the huge sutra of visions behind them. Today's word is its name: Avatamsaka, the Flower Garland.
screen: `DEW ON A WEB.` → `EACH DROP HOLDS ANOTHER.` → `THE FLOWER GARLAND.`

segments.voice: The Avatamsaka Sutra, usually called the Flower Garland in English, isn't built like an argument. It's built like a vision. Buddhas fill worlds, light pours from them, and the scenes keep opening inside one another. In China a school grew up around it, called Huayan, which is the Chinese name of the sutra, and its teachers needed pictures for what the sutra was showing. One is Indra's net. As Huayan tells it, in the heaven of the god Indra hangs a net stretching out in every direction. At every knot there's a jewel, polished so clear that it reflects every other jewel in the net, and each of those reflections holds the reflections of all the others, without end. Look into one jewel and you're looking at the entire net. The point isn't only that everything is connected. A string of causes is connected too: the farmer, the rain, the truck, the cup of coffee. Huayan says more. Each thing actually holds the whole. One in all, all in one. And here's the detail that's easy to miss: the jewels don't melt into one big glow. Each stays a single jewel in its own place, and that's exactly why it can reflect the others. Tradition says a Huayan teacher once showed this to a ruler of China by setting mirrors all around a lamp, so the one flame appeared everywhere at once. The net shows up in small places too: one person's mood filling a whole room, a whole family visible in one child's face.
screen: `A SUTRA BUILT LIKE A VISION.` · `A NET OF JEWELS IN INDRA'S HEAVEN.` · `EACH JEWEL SHOWS THE WHOLE NET.` · `EACH JEWEL STAYS ITSELF.` · then, large: `EACH REFLECTS ALL.`

segments.voice: Find something that reflects: a window, a glass of water, a dark phone screen, the back of a spoon. Look at what's caught there, then look again more slowly, and notice the glass showing things it isn't while staying exactly itself. If a second surface is nearby, see whether one shows the other.
Avatamsaka. The Flower Garland Sutra, whose Huayan teachers pictured everything as a net of jewels, each one reflecting all the rest. Today's word.
Your line: each reflects all. The smallest drop on the web holds the whole garden. Rest well.

1194.title: Sudhana's pilgrimage
1194.hook: a young seeker visits fifty-three teachers, among them a monk, a girl, a sailor and a king (Flower Garland, Gandavyuha)
1194.howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism, Sudhana's journey is told as a model of seeking good spiritual friends, and his meetings with his teachers have been painted and carved in temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indra's net: a jewel at every knot, each one shining with all the others. Your line: each reflects all.

Who taught you the thing you actually live by? Not the answer you'd put on a form; the real one. Sometimes it's somebody nobody would have hired as a teacher: a grandmother, a coach, a bus driver, the kid at the next desk. A long section of the Flower Garland Sutra, called the Gandavyuha, is built on that surprise. A young man named Sudhana, the seeker carved on the walls of Borobudur, wants to learn how a bodhisattva lives. Instead of settling with one master, he sets off walking.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU, REALLY?` → `NOT ALWAYS A TEACHER.` → `SUDHANA SETS OFF WALKING.`

segments.voice: It begins with Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. He sees how much Sudhana wants to learn, and he doesn't hand him the whole teaching. He tells him to go and find good friends, spiritual friends, and to ask each one how to follow the bodhisattva's way. Then he points him to the first. So Sudhana walks. And his teachers aren't who you'd expect. There's a monk, yes. There's also a sailor who knows the sea and its dangers, a girl, laywomen and householders, a perfume seller, a boy, a king. Some are calm and gentle. A few are startling, and Sudhana has to wonder whether he's come to the right place. Tradition counts fifty-three of them. The same pattern repeats, teacher after teacher. Sudhana arrives, bows and asks. The teacher tells him what they know: one practice, one door into the way, opened as far as they've opened it. Then, more or less: this is the door I know. I can't tell you about the rest. Go on to the next. However great the teacher, nobody keeps him, and nobody claims to have the whole of it. Wisdom isn't stored in one famous person on one mountain. It's spread out, a piece in a harbor, a piece in a palace, a piece in a shop. Sudhana's whole job is to keep walking, keep asking, and bow to whoever is standing in front of him. The next teacher might be the person about to be hurried past.

segments.voice: Let a memory come of someone who taught you something without meaning to: a stranger on a train, a remark from a coworker, a sentence overheard in a waiting room. Stay with that moment and ask what door they opened that you hadn't found. Then leave the question open, the way Sudhana kept walking.

1195.title: Maitreya's tower
1195.hook: Sudhana enters a tower where every room holds all the others
1195.howItsDone: Readers of the Flower Garland Sutra in East Asian Buddhism treat Sudhana's vision in Maitreya's tower as a high point of his pilgrimage and a picture of how all things contain one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sudhana walked from teacher to teacher: a monk, a girl, a sailor, a king. Your line: fifty-three teachers.

The door is shut. Sudhana stands outside a great tower, at the end of city after city and teacher after teacher, and he can't get in. So he waits. He walks around it with respect, and he hopes. Then the owner comes up the road with a crowd around him. It's Maitreya, the bodhisattva who, Buddhists say, will be the next Buddha, the same Maitreya from Asanga's story. Sudhana asks to be let in, and what happens next turns the whole road inside out.
screen: `A SHUT DOOR.` → `SUDHANA WAITS.` → `MAITREYA COMES UP THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Maitreya doesn't use a key. He snaps his fingers, and the door opens. Sudhana steps in, the door closes behind him, and the inside is bigger than the outside. Much bigger. The tower is as wide as the sky, and within it are other towers, more than he can count, each one as vast and as beautifully made. Here's the part to slow down for. Those towers don't crowd each other. Each one is whole, and each sits inside the others without pushing anything out of the way. Every room holds all the rooms, and every room is still its own. In them Sudhana sees scenes from Maitreya's long path: Maitreya first setting out, practicing, teaching, giving. He even sees himself there, standing in front of each scene. A few days ago, Indra's net was a picture to think about. Here, the young pilgrim walks around inside it. Then Maitreya snaps his fingers again, and the vision is over. Sudhana is standing in an ordinary tower. Where did it all go, he asks. Maitreya's answer is gentle. It didn't come from anywhere, and it hasn't gone anywhere. It arose from conditions, the way a dream does, or a magic show, and it rests the same way. In the sutra's telling, it isn't a trick to fool Sudhana. It's how everything works, shown all at once. A kitchen can hold every meal ever cooked in it, a song can hold a whole summer, and neither gets any larger.
screen: `MAITREYA SNAPS HIS FINGERS.` · `TOWERS INSIDE THE TOWER.` · `NOTHING CROWDS ANYTHING.` · `ANOTHER SNAP, AND IT'S GONE.` · then, large: `EVERY ROOM HOLDS ALL.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand in your lap and look at it. Let it open the way the tower did: every hand it has held, every meal it has lifted, every door it has opened, years of days inside it without the hand growing any bigger. Then come back to just the hand, resting there, its own size.
Maitreya's tower. The tower Sudhana enters at a snap of the fingers, where every tower holds all the others. Today's word.
Your line: every room holds all. A snap of the fingers, and the road turned inside out. I'll be here tomorrow.

1196.title: The whole in a grain
1196.hook: a world in a grain of dust, all time in a moment
1196.howItsDone: Huayan teachers in China drew on these passages of the Flower Garland Sutra to describe a world in which the small and the large, and a moment and an age, contain each other without obstruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreya snapped his fingers, and Sudhana walked into a tower where towers held towers. Your line: every room holds all.

One grain of rice is left on the table after dinner. A thumb is already on its way to brush it off. The Flower Garland Sutra would like that thumb to pause. It says something that sounds impossible: inside a single speck of dust there are whole worlds, with Buddhas teaching in them, and inside one moment there are ages upon ages of time. Yesterday a tower held towers. Today it gets smaller, and stranger.
screen: `ONE GRAIN ON THE TABLE.` → `WORLDS IN A SPECK OF DUST.` → `AGES IN A MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Start with space. The sutra pictures a speck of dust, almost too small to see, and inside it, worlds beyond counting, each with its lands and its beings and a Buddha teaching there. Here's the careful part. The speck doesn't swell up to make room, and the worlds don't shrink down to fit. Each stays exactly its own size, and still the one holds the many. Huayan teachers in China had a phrase for this: big and small don't obstruct each other. Then time. One instant of thought holds vast ages, and vast ages fit inside one instant, and neither is squeezed. Past, present and future can be found in a single moment, the way the whole net is found in a single jewel. Why would anyone say this? Because in this way of seeing, nothing has a fixed size or a fixed edge of its own. Things exist through each other. A grain of rice isn't a little sealed box. It's made of a field, of rain and sun and soil, of hands that planted and hands that harvested, of the trucks and the store and the pot. That's the gentle version. The sutra goes further: the grain isn't only linked to everything; the whole is present in it. So the small thing on the table, about to be brushed away, isn't small in the way it looks. That can change how a crumb gets swept, or how one ordinary minute gets spent.
screen: `WORLDS INSIDE A SPECK OF DUST.` · `NOTHING SHRINKS, NOTHING SWELLS.` · `AGES INSIDE ONE MOMENT.` · `THE GRAIN ON THE TABLE.` · then, large: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Put something tiny where you can see it: a grain of rice or salt, a crumb, a speck of dust. Look at it longer than feels normal, its color and its edges. Then let it open: where did it come from, who touched it on the way, what weather made it? Let this one grain be enough.
The whole in a grain. The Flower Garland's teaching that a speck of dust holds worlds, and one moment holds ages, without either changing size. Today's word.

1197.title: The finger and the moon
1197.hook: a finger pointing at the moon is not the moon: words point, they are not the thing (Lankavatara)
1197.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers, and especially Chan and Zen teachers, use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras and explanations point toward awakening and are not awakening itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, worlds in a speck of dust, and ages in one moment. Your line: a world in a grain.

Someone stands in a dark yard, points up and says: look, the moon. And the person beside them stares hard at the end of the finger. Fingernail. Knuckle. A little ink stain. It's a small joke, and the Lankavatara Sutra uses it to say something serious about every word of teaching, its own words included. It's also a good way to end this week.
screen: `LOOK, THE MOON.` → `STARING AT THE FINGER.` → `ABOUT EVERY WORD OF TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the picture, as the Lankavatara gives it. When someone points out the moon with a fingertip, a foolish person looks at the fingertip and not at the moon. In the same way, the sutra says, people who cling to the letter of the teaching, to the words alone, don't see the truth the words are pointing at. Two things are true at once. First, the finger is needed. Without someone pointing, nobody looks up. The sutra isn't telling anyone to throw words away; teachings, texts and explanations are how anyone finds the direction at all. Second, the finger is not the moon. A person can learn every word, repeat every line, argue every point, and still be staring at a knuckle. The Lankavatara comes back to this difference between the words and the meaning. Some later Chan and Zen teachers picked up the image too. Now look back at this week, a week of fingers. A goddess switched bodies with Shariputra, pointing at labels that aren't fixed. Vimalakirti pointed with silence. Then a net of jewels, a young man walking from teacher to teacher, a tower full of towers, a world in a grain. Each one is a finger, aimed somewhere. None of them is the moon. They're there so the eyes can travel past them. The test is small: after hearing something wise, does the attention stay on the clever words, or move on to what they were pointing at?
screen: `A FOOL LOOKS AT THE FINGERTIP.` · `THE FINGER IS NEEDED.` · `THE FINGER IS NOT THE MOON.` · `A WEEK OF FINGERS.` · then, large: `NOT THE FINGER.`

segments.voice: Point at the sky if you can see it, or at a lamp or a window. Look at the finger for a breath, then let your eyes move past it to what it points at, and lower the hand. Now let the word go too, not lamp, not sky, just this light, here.
The finger and the moon. The Lankavatara's picture of words as a finger pointing: needed, but never the thing itself. Today's word.
